steps.premise: Later arrivals may look just like the student's bowls.
steps.action: Keep a pencil and reusable name cards at the rack so the student can label the board as soon as they put it down.
steps.consequence: The board is identified while its contents are still recognizable.
steps.quote: A student should be able to put their name on a board while they still know which of a dozen lookalike bowls is theirs. A pencil and a supply of reusable name cards right at the rack let them claim the board before the other bowls arrive.

steps.premise: Beginners need a way to judge spacing before loading a board.
steps.action: Show pots on the teaching table spaced far enough apart for a hand to pass between them.
steps.consequence: Students have an example of how much room to leave on their own boards.
steps.quote: On the teaching table, set out a board of pots with enough space to slip a hand between neighbors. Beginners can use it to judge the gaps as they get ready to fill their own boards.

steps.premise: Some shelves extend beyond comfortable reach from the front.
steps.action: Keep the area behind those shelves accessible.
steps.consequence: People can reach the back pots without leaning across fresh rims.
steps.quote: If a shelf is deeper than a person can comfortably reach, keep the space behind it clear so they can reach the far pots without leaning over freshly made rims.

steps.premise: A low dish at the back of a dim shelf may be overlooked.
steps.action: Aim a small light along the back of the shelf.
steps.consequence: People can see the dish in a space that otherwise looks vacant.
steps.quote: On a dark shelf, point a small light along the back so a low dish is easy to spot even where the shelf looks empty.

steps.premise: An empty board and a board of drying work have different uses.
steps.action: Put spare boards on a dedicated stand near the worktables.
steps.consequence: Students can distinguish available boards from boards in use.
steps.quote: Give spare boards their own stand by the worktables so students can tell supplies from work taking up drying space.

steps.premise: A member's pots may need attention during their absence.
steps.action: Have the absent member designate someone to check on the pots.
steps.consequence: Staff know who can help with that member's work.
steps.quote: Members who will be away can name someone to look in on their pots. Then staff know whom to ask if one needs attention.

steps.premise: An organizer needs to know whether the event can be seated on a particular day.
steps.action: Show the number of available chairs for each date in the shared calendar.
steps.consequence: The organizer can check the supply against the event's needs.
steps.quote: An organizer looking up a date in the shared booking calendar should see how many chairs are free that day and be able to tell if there are enough for the event.

steps.premise: A delayed driver may still need access during the event.
steps.action: Ask each organizer to name a person who can answer the phone and has the keys then.
steps.consequence: The driver has a reachable contact who can provide access.
steps.quote: Ask each organizer for the name of someone who can take a call and has the keys during the event, in case the delivery driver is delayed.

steps.premise: The organizer might leave before the chairs are due back.
steps.action: When making return arrangements, allow the borrower to name another person to bring them back.
steps.consequence: The agreed return time can still be met.
steps.quote: When borrowers arrange the return, let them designate someone else to bring the chairs back. That keeps the agreed time workable even if the organizer leaves early.

steps.premise: The team needs to mark reserved seats without leaving adhesive on borrowed chairs.
steps.action: Supply row signs that clip on and can be removed after the event.
steps.consequence: The chairs return without tape or residue.
steps.quote: Supply row signs the event team can clip on to reserve seats and take off afterward, so the borrowed chairs come back free of tape and sticky residue.

steps.premise: Chairs are sometimes returned too wet to store.
steps.action: Provide a covered place to leave returned chairs open.
steps.consequence: They can dry there until ready for storage.
steps.quote: If chairs come back wet, have a spot under cover where they can stand open until they're dry enough to store.

steps.premise: A returned chair with a loose hinge or missing foot could be sent out again by mistake.
steps.action: Attach a conspicuous repair tag and keep that chair apart from the others.
steps.consequence: It stays out of the next delivery.
steps.quote: Should a chair have a loose hinge or be missing a foot, put a repair tag where it's easy to see and store the chair separately so it won't go out with the next load.

steps.premise: A sound may explain why the speakers react or fall silent.
steps.action: Briefly name a sound in the captions when it matters to the exchange.
steps.consequence: Visitors can understand the speakers' response.
steps.quote: Think about what a visitor needs to understand a pause or a change of voice. If both speakers break off to listen to a train whistle, a short caption naming the sound helps explain their reaction. Do the same for other sounds when they matter to the exchange.

steps.premise: The narrator sometimes switches to reading another person's words.
steps.action: Introduce a letter or diary excerpt in the captions as reading starts and identify its author.
steps.consequence: Visitors know whose words they are following.
steps.quote: As soon as the narrator begins reading from a letter or diary, use the captions to introduce the passage and identify whose words the visitor is hearing.

steps.premise: Visitors need to grasp phrases and recognize full names quickly.
steps.action: Break caption lines at natural phrases and keep both parts of a person's name together.
steps.consequence: A reader can take in the words and names at a glance.
steps.quote: Choose line breaks that follow the phrasing of the sentence, and put each person's given name and surname on the same line so visitors can read them at a glance.

steps.premise: An answer may appear unprompted to a viewer following the captions alone.
steps.action: Have a reviewer watch the whole interview muted and flag answers that seem to lack a lead-in.
steps.consequence: The review identifies places where that viewer lacks context.
steps.quote: Have a reviewer watch an interview from beginning to end on mute and mark any answer that seems to have no lead-in.

steps.premise: Someone entering a looping exhibit may miss the beginning.
steps.action: Keep the interview title in view next to the captions.
steps.consequence: Visitors can identify the story at any point.
steps.quote: In a looping exhibit, keep the interview title visible beside the captions so people can identify the story even if they come in halfway through.

steps.premise: Staff need to find the particular error a visitor spotted.
steps.action: Ask for the interview title and the time shown on the player on the correction slip.
steps.consequence: Staff can locate the reported passage.
steps.quote: Visitors who catch an error can help staff locate it if the correction slip prompts them for the interview title and the time on the player.

steps.premise: A first-time guest may arrive without seeing anyone familiar.
steps.action: Have a host greet them at the door and offer to walk with them to the lesson.
steps.consequence: They meet someone immediately and do not have to search the room.
steps.quote: Give newcomers someone to meet right away. A host at the door can offer to walk them to the lesson, so a first-time guest doesn't have to scan the room for someone they know.

steps.premise: Newcomers may be unsure what to say when invited to dance.
steps.action: During the welcome, demonstrate an invitation and a friendly decline.
steps.consequence: People hear how the interaction can end comfortably whichever answer they give.
steps.quote: During the welcome, act out asking someone to dance and turning down a dance in a friendly way. Let people hear how comfortably the exchange can end whichever answer they give.

steps.premise: Beginners need a moment to choose whether to participate.
steps.action: Announce the upcoming dance before the song starts.
steps.consequence: They can decide before the dancing begins.
steps.quote: Before a song begins, tell the room which dance is coming up so beginners have a moment to decide whether to join in.

steps.premise: Spoken instruction can be hard to hear.
steps.action: Illuminate the teacher's face and feet during demonstrations.
steps.consequence: Guests can follow the demonstration visually.
steps.quote: Light the teacher's face as well as their feet during demonstrations, so people can follow by sight when it's hard to hear.

steps.premise: Spinning can feel uncomfortable for some guests.
steps.action: Also demonstrate a simple version of the turn that keeps both feet low.
steps.consequence: Those guests have a way to finish the figure.
steps.quote: For a turn, also teach a simple way to complete the figure with both feet low to the floor for anyone who finds spinning uncomfortable.

steps.premise: Guests who sit out several songs may miss chances to meet people.
steps.action: Turn the music down for a short break and invite everyone to talk.
steps.consequence: Even someone who has skipped dances can make acquaintances.
steps.quote: Lower the music for a break and invite everyone to chat for a few minutes. A guest who has sat out several dances can still make some acquaintances that evening.

steps.premise: A neighbor without an oven may still know a local bread worth sharing.
steps.action: Publicize that loaves from a favorite neighborhood bakery are welcome.
steps.consequence: That neighbor can contribute a bread for others to discover.
steps.quote: Make it clear that people can bring a loaf from a neighborhood bakery they love. A neighbor who has no oven might introduce everyone to a bread just as interesting as one baked at home.

steps.premise: A guest may arrive empty-handed after a batch fails.
steps.action: Set aside extra contributions in a basket for people without bread to trade.
steps.consequence: They can still participate in the swap that evening.
steps.quote: Keep some extra contributions in a basket for guests who arrive with nothing to swap, so a batch of dough that failed to rise needn't cost someone an evening with the group.

steps.premise: A newcomer may be uncertain how much bread makes a fair portion.
steps.action: Display a real piece cut to the suggested size at the entrance.
steps.consequence: The newcomer can see how much to offer.
steps.quote: At the entrance, display an actual piece of bread cut to the suggested swap size. It spares a newcomer the awkward guess about how much is fair.

steps.premise: A crust can hide unfamiliar fillings or toppings.
steps.action: Provide blank cards beside the loaves with space for contributors to describe those ingredients.
steps.consequence: Guests can learn what is in or on a loaf from its card.
steps.quote: Lay out blank ingredient cards alongside the loaves, with enough space to describe fillings and toppings that people may have trouble recognizing from the crust.

steps.premise: Starting a conversation with a whole group can feel awkward.
steps.action: Invite each contributor to leave a short note on the bread's history.
steps.consequence: Guests have a specific story they can ask the baker about.
steps.quote: Encourage contributors to leave a short note about the history of their bread, too. Asking a baker about their grandmother's skillet bread can feel easier than introducing yourself to everyone at once.

steps.premise: Standing for a long time can be tiring.
steps.action: Put a stool by the exchange table.
steps.consequence: A guest can stay and talk with bakers while seated.
steps.quote: A stool beside the exchange table lets someone who finds standing tiring stay a while and talk with the bakers.

steps.premise: Visitors may hesitate to make an imperfect mark in a public book.
steps.action: Ask a gardener to leave an unfinished pencil sketch near the front.
steps.consequence: Seeing tentative marks already on the page makes contributing feel easier.
steps.quote: Near the start of a book, invite a gardener to leave a pencil sketch that's still in progress. Seeing someone else's tentative lines can make it easier to risk an imperfect one on a page everyone will see.

steps.premise: Some people want to test a stroke before anyone sees it.
steps.action: Place paper scraps in the pencil tray.
steps.consequence: Visitors can try their marks privately first.
steps.quote: Tuck a few scraps of paper into the pencil tray for anyone who'd like to try out a stroke in private first.

steps.premise: A whole garden border may seem too large for one page.
steps.action: Offer a small cardboard viewfinder that frames a patch of stems.
steps.consequence: The visitor can choose a smaller scene to draw.
steps.quote: For a visitor wondering how to fit a whole border on one page, offer a little cardboard viewfinder to frame a patch of stems.

steps.premise: Visitors may want a close view of the subject's details.
steps.action: Offer fallen pods on the table as drawing subjects.
steps.consequence: People can inspect details without picking plants.
steps.quote: The fallen pods on the table make another good invitation to draw. Visitors can get close to the details without picking anything.

steps.premise: Someone looking through the book may want to see a sketched plant firsthand.
steps.action: Leave space next to the drawing to record where the plant grows.
steps.consequence: The reader can find it in the garden and examine it.
steps.quote: Beside each sketch, leave room to say where in the garden the plant grows, so a reader taken with a particular seed head can find it and look more closely.

steps.premise: Some visitors like to observe in silence while others draw nearby.
steps.action: Occasionally reserve quiet drawing time before a garden tour.
steps.consequence: They can share the sketchbooks in quiet company.
steps.quote: Occasionally set aside quiet drawing time before a garden tour, so visitors who enjoy observing in silence can use the books together.

steps.premise: A performer may be delayed on the way to a fitting.
steps.action: Give performers a named contact who can relay news of a delay.
steps.consequence: The team may have time to use the empty appointment slot.
steps.quote: Give performers one contact by name who can pass on word if they're held up on the way. The team may still have time to use the vacant slot.

steps.premise: A fitter needs to track time while tending to the wearer.
steps.action: Position an easy-to-read clock within the fitter's sight.
steps.consequence: The fitter can pace the appointment without repeatedly looking away.
steps.quote: Put a clearly legible clock where the fitter can see it while attending to the performer, so they can keep the appointment on pace without repeatedly turning away.

steps.premise: Owners can restrict changes to borrowed garments, for example by requiring that a hem be restorable.
steps.action: Label each borrowed garment on the rail with the changes its owner permits.
steps.consequence: A volunteer can check those limits before making the alteration.
steps.quote: On the rail, label each borrowed piece with the alterations its owner allows. A volunteer can then see that a hem has to go back exactly as it came before taking it up.

steps.premise: At the end of the night, finished clothes may get mixed up with pieces still needing alterations.
steps.action: Give stage-ready garments a separate rail.
steps.consequence: They stay distinct when the team gathers work still to do.
steps.quote: Set aside a separate rail for stage-ready clothes so they won't get swept in with work awaiting alterations at the end of the night.

steps.premise: Some changes require the wearer to come back, and the garment and the wearer's schedule are available at the current fitting.
steps.action: Circle those changes and agree on the return time with the wearer there.
steps.consequence: The necessary second fitting is identified and scheduled.
steps.quote: Circle changes that call for a second fitting and settle the return time with the wearer while the garment is there and they have their schedule handy.

steps.premise: There may be more sewing than the team has time for.
steps.action: Record the order of priority agreed by the team when time is short.
steps.consequence: A costume needed for the next rehearsal can receive attention in time.
steps.quote: If the sewing list outgrows the time available, record which jobs everyone agrees should come first so the costume for tomorrow's rehearsal gets worked on in time.

steps.premise: Arriving visitors want to judge how busy the tables are before going into the playing area.
steps.action: Keep the view from the doorway unobstructed.
steps.consequence: Visitors can see table occupancy before stepping in.
steps.quote: From the doorway, visitors should be able to see how busy the tables are before they step into the playing area, so keep that view clear.

steps.premise: A learner may hesitate to ask a question during play if unsure whether the opponent minds.
steps.action: Reserve a couple of tables for games where spoken questions are welcome.
steps.consequence: Learners at those tables can ask about a move with confidence.
steps.quote: Dedicate a couple of tables to games where it's fine to ask questions out loud. Someone learning can then ask about a move without having to work out whether their opponent will mind.

steps.premise: Explaining a position at a live match can draw a crowd around the players.
steps.action: Put a demonstration board in a corner away from current games.
steps.consequence: A helper can set up and discuss the position away from someone else's match.
steps.quote: A demonstration board in a corner away from games in progress lets a helper set up a position and talk it through without drawing people around somebody else's match.

steps.premise: Children learning how the pieces move need pieces they can handle.
steps.action: Give them a separate set to practise with.
steps.consequence: They can test moves without borrowing pieces from an ongoing game.
steps.quote: Give children who want to work on moving the pieces a set they can use themselves. They can try out the knight's jump without taking pieces from a game in progress.

steps.premise: A clock beeping at the end of a nearby game can break concentration.
steps.action: Silence the shared chess clocks.
steps.consequence: Other players can stay focused as games finish.
steps.quote: Turn off the beeps on the shared clocks so players can keep concentrating when the game next to them ends.

steps.premise: A beginner may have trouble estimating how much playing time remains before closing.
steps.action: Quietly alert the players before the room closes.
steps.consequence: They have time to agree with their opponent where to stop.
steps.quote: A quiet word to the players before the room closes gives a beginner who's still getting a feel for how long games take time to agree with their opponent on where to stop.
